section: Loading and Cleaning Data for Synthetic Dataset
text:
Loading and Cleaning Data for Synthetic Dataset

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
set.seed(1234)

raw <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("cdcdata-exercise", "cdc_obesity_2018plus.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
stopifnot(nrow(raw) > 0)


dat <- raw %>% # saves raw data as dat for next steps in synth creation
  transmute( # creates new dataset with same variables as in original, with cleaned names and formatting
    year = YearStart,
    state = LocationAbbr,
    location = LocationDesc,
    question = Question,
    value = Data_Value,
    unit = Data_Value_Unit,
    value_type = Data_Value_Type,
    sex = Sex,
    age_group = `Age(years)`
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, ""))) %>% # if values are empty strings, convert to NA for consistency in handling missing data
  filter(!is.na(value)) # removes rows where value var is missing


# Reproducibility: set seed for any random processes
set.seed(1234) # original seed was 2026, changed it because i prefer simple numbers.
# Reproducibility
set.seed(1234)

# Ensure Part 1 object exists
stopifnot(exists("dat"))

# helper: sample from observed distribution including NA
# helper makes synthetic data preserve the same distribution of values (including missingness) as the original data
sample_like <- function(x, n) {
  tx <- table(x, useNA = "ifany") # counts how often each value (including NA) appears in the original data
  p  <- as.numeric(tx) / sum(tx) # coverts counts to probabilities/proportions
  lv <- names(tx) # saves the unique values (including NA) as a character vector
  s  <- sample(lv, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = p)
  ifelse(s == "<NA>", NA, s) # converts string "<NA>" back to actual NA values in the synthetic data
}

n_rows <- nrow(dat) # stores the number of rows in the original dataset so synth dataset can copy.

# keep valid state-location pairs
state_location_map <- dat %>%
  filter(!is.na(state), !is.na(location)) %>%
  distinct(state, location)

# build synthetic scaffold (without value first)
dat_syn <- tibble(
  year       = as.numeric(sample_like(dat$year, n_rows)),
  state      = sample_like(dat$state, n_rows),
  question   = sample_like(dat$question, n_rows),
  unit       = sample_like(dat$unit, n_rows),
  value_type = sample_like(dat$value_type, n_rows),
  sex        = sample_like(dat$sex, n_rows),
  age_group  = sample_like(dat$age_group, n_rows)
) %>%
  left_join(state_location_map, by = "state")

# fallback if any missing locations remain
if (any(is.na(dat_syn$location))) {
  dat_syn$location[is.na(dat_syn$location)] <-
    sample_like(dat$location, sum(is.na(dat_syn$location))) # fills in any missing locations by sampling from the original location distribution, ensuring all rows have a location value.
}


# now we can check out the synthetic dataset and compare it to the original
glimpse(dat_syn) # check syn dataset structure

$ sex        <chr> NA, "Female", NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, N…

# Simulate value using subgroup stats + global fallback
g_mean <- mean(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)
g_sd   <- sd(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)
v_min  <- min(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)
v_max  <- max(dat$value, na.rm = TRUE)

# subgroup means/sd by question + sex + age group
# Chatgpt recommeneded grouping to make synth data more realistic by preserving original data patterns. Can be skipped though...
grp <- dat %>%
  group_by(question, sex, age_group) %>%
  summarise(
    mu = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# add subgroup params to synthetic rows and simulate value
dat_syn <- dat_syn %>%
  left_join(grp, by = c("question", "sex", "age_group")) %>%
  mutate(
    mu = ifelse(is.na(mu), g_mean, mu),
    sd = ifelse(is.na(sd) | sd <= 0, g_sd, sd),
    value = rnorm(n(), mean = mu, sd = sd),
    value = pmax(v_min, pmin(v_max, value))
  ) %>%
  select(year, state, location, question, value, unit, value_type, sex, age_group)


# quick checks

Descriptive Summaries with Synthetic Data
Now we can compare the descriptive summaries of the original and synthetic datasets to see how well the synthetic data mimics the original. I’ve pulled the code from the original EDA section for easy comparison. For the prompt, I asked: Now that we have the synthetic dataset, I want to compare the descriptive summaries (I pasted summaries code).

cat_vars <- c("state", "sex", "age_group", "value_type", "unit")

for (v in cat_vars) {
  cat("\n====================\n")
  cat("Variable:", v, "\n")
  cat("====================\n")
  
  comp_wide <- bind_rows(
    dat %>% count(.data[[v]], name = "n") %>% mutate(dataset = "original"),
    dat_syn %>% count(.data[[v]], name = "n") %>% mutate(dataset = "synthetic")
  ) %>%
    group_by(dataset) %>%
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(value = .data[[v]], dataset, n, pct) %>% # pivot wider converges the original and synthetic summaries into a single table for side-by-side comparison
    # I had to add pivot wider because Chatgpt's original code printed them one after another and it was visually gross to look at... 
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = dataset,
      values_from = c(n, pct)
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      diff_pct = pct_synthetic - pct_original
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(abs(diff_pct)))
  
  print(comp_wide, n = 20)
  cat("\n")
}

text:
Figures with Synthetic Data
Finally, we can also compare the figures of the original and synthetic datasets side by side. For the prompt: Now i want to compare the figures of my synthetic data to the original data side by side. lets do this 1 figure at a time (then i pasted the original code).

bind_rows(
  dat %>% mutate(dataset = "Original"),
  dat_syn %>% mutate(dataset = "Synthetic")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_wrap(~ dataset, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of value: Original vs Synthetic",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Count"
  )








Figure 1 shows that we maintained the same distribution of value in the synthetic data! Our peak is slightly smaller and the tail is a bit shorter, but the overall shape is very similar. Huzzah!
For the next prompt I asked: Now i want to do figure 2. I want to split it so that distribution of value by sex has original Female figure beside synthetic Female figure, original Male by synthetic Male.

bind_rows( # binds original and synthetic datasets together for faceting
  dat %>% mutate(dataset = "Original"),
  dat_syn %>% mutate(dataset = "Synthetic")
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(sex), sex %in% c("Female", "Male")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_grid(sex ~ dataset) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = range(c(dat$value, dat_syn$value), na.rm = TRUE)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of value by sex",
    subtitle = "Original vs Synthetic", # Chatgpt did not fix titles so I adjusted title and created a subtitle for clarity
    x = "Value",
    y = "Count"
  )








Figure 2 also shows that the synthetic data mimics the original data well within each sex group. The distributions for both Female and Male in the synthetic data resemble those in the original data. title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
2.1 Research Question
The primary research question for this study is: Are individuals who report being asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal care less likely to report postpartum depressive symptoms? The primary outcome of interest is self-reported postpartum depressive symptoms, measured using PRAMS survey items assessing feelings of depression and loss of interest since birth. The primary predictor of interest is prenatal mental health screening, defined by whether a healthcare provider asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal visits. Additional covariates considered for analysis include depression during pregnancy and maternal education.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
3.1 Use of Computational Assistance
Artificial intelligence tool (ChatGPT) was used to assist with code troubleshooting. All code and analytical decisions were reviewed, modified as needed, and implemented by the author. The author takes full responsibility for the accuracy, interpretation, and reproducibility of all analyses and results.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
3.2 Analysis Approach
The analysis plan included descriptive summaries of key variables and exploratory comparisons between individuals who did and did not report prenatal mental health screening. These exploratory analyses were used to assess data quality, missingness, and preliminary patterns in the data.
Regression-based and model validation approaches were then used to examine associations between prenatal screening and postpartum mental health outcomes while accounting for relevant covariates.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
3.3 Data Source
Data were obtained from the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS), a population-based surveillance system conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in collaboration with state health departments. PRAMS collects self-reported information on maternal experiences before, during, and shortly after pregnancy.
Because PRAMS uses a complex survey design, weighted analyses can be conducted using the survey design variables provided in the dataset. However, the results presented here focus on descriptive summaries and logistic regression models based on the analytic dataset used for the project.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
3.5 Measures
The primary exposure in this study was self-reported prenatal mental health screening, measured using a PRAMS survey item indicating whether a healthcare provider asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal care. This variable was coded as a binary indicator representing whether respondents reported being screened during prenatal visits.
The primary outcome was postpartum depressive symptoms. PRAMS includes survey items assessing whether respondents experienced feelings consistent with depression or loss of interest following childbirth. These items have been used in previous research examining postpartum depressive symptoms using PRAMS data Bauman et al. (2020); Farr et al. (2016).
Key covariates included depression during pregnancy (BPG_DEPRS8) and maternal education (MAT_ED). Depression during pregnancy was included as an important potential confounder, as individuals with a history of depression may be more likely to experience postpartum depressive symptoms. Maternal education was included as a sociodemographic variable that may influence both healthcare experiences and mental health outcomes.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
3.6 Statistical Approach
Exploratory analyses included descriptive statistics, cross-tabulations, and graphical comparisons of postpartum depressive symptoms by screening status. All analyses were conducted in R.
Multivariable logistic regression models were specified with postpartum depressive symptoms as the binary outcome. Prenatal mental health screening was included as the primary exposure. Covariates included depression during pregnancy and maternal education. Results are presented as odds ratios with corresponding 95% confidence intervals.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.1 Exploratory Analysis
We first examined the distribution of prenatal mental health screening and postpartum depressive symptoms in the analytic sample. We also explored how postpartum depressive symptoms varied by screening status, depression during pregnancy, and maternal education.
Descriptive results suggested that postpartum depressive symptoms were more common among respondents who did not report receiving prenatal mental health screening. Higher rates of postpartum depressive symptoms were also observed among respondents who reported depression during pregnancy. Differences across maternal education groups were also examined to assess potential patterns in the data.
These exploratory analyses helped identify initial patterns in the dataset and informed the selection of variables for adjusted modeling.

title: Prenatal Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depressive Symptoms
text:
4.2 Discussion
This study evaluated the association between prenatal mental health screening and postpartum depressive symptoms using population-based PRAMS data. Respondents who reported prenatal mental health screening had lower odds of postpartum depressive symptoms than those who were not screened, even after adjustment for depression during pregnancy and maternal education.
Although PRAMS includes survey weights and design variables, the analyses presented here are unweighted and intended as an exploratory course project focused on reproducible modeling workflows.
These findings are generally consistent with existing research showing that postpartum depressive symptoms remain a significant public health concern in the United States. Previous analyses using PRAMS data have documented that a substantial proportion of women report postpartum depressive symptoms and that provider discussions about perinatal depression vary across populations and healthcare settings Bauman et al. (2020); Farr et al. (2016). Clinical guidelines from organizations such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend routine screening for depression during pregnancy and the postpartum period to support earlier identification and intervention American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (2023).
The exploratory results from this study suggest that prenatal screening may be associated with differences in postpartum mental health outcomes at the population level. However, these results should be interpreted cautiously. Because the data are observational and based on self-reported survey responses, the analyses cannot determine whether prenatal screening itself reduces postpartum depressive symptoms. It is possible that individuals who receive more comprehensive prenatal care are also more likely to receive screening and additional support services that influence postpartum mental health outcomes.
Depression during pregnancy emerged as one of the strongest predictors of postpartum depressive symptoms in the adjusted analyses. This finding aligns with previous research showing that mental health history is an important risk factor for postpartum depression. Accounting for prior depression is therefore essential when examining associations between prenatal care experiences and postpartum mental health outcomes.
Several strengths of this study should be noted. PRAMS provides a large, population-based dataset that captures maternal experiences across multiple states. The survey includes detailed information on prenatal care experiences, health behaviors, and postpartum outcomes, allowing researchers to examine mental health patterns at a population level. The large sample size also supports exploratory regression analyses and the evaluation of multiple potential confounders.
This study also has several limitations. First, PRAMS data are self-reported and may be subject to recall bias or reporting bias. Second, the postpartum depressive symptom measure used in PRAMS is not a clinical diagnosis of depression but rather a survey-based indicator of depressive symptoms. Third, the cross-sectional nature of the survey limits the ability to determine temporal relationships or causal effects. Finally, unmeasured factors such as healthcare access, provider practices, or social support may influence both screening and postpartum mental health outcomes.
Despite these limitations, the findings highlight the potential value of examining prenatal mental health screening practices using population-based surveillance data. Understanding how screening practices relate to maternal mental health outcomes may help inform future research and public health efforts aimed at improving maternal mental health.
Future analyses could expand on this work by incorporating additional covariates such as insurance status, socioeconomic indicators, and access to mental health services. More advanced modeling approaches could also be used to explore predictors of postpartum depressive symptoms and identify subgroups that may benefit most from screening and early intervention.
Overall, this study demonstrates how large surveillance datasets such as PRAMS can be used to explore maternal mental health patterns and generate hypotheses for future research. Continued attention to perinatal mental health remains important for improving maternal and infant health outcomes.
